items.lawCode: Amd §2872, add §2874-b, Pub Health L; amd §§3 & 5, add §7-c, NYS Med Care Fac Fin Ag Act
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S5562

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the public health law and the New York state medical
care facilities finance agency act, in relation to providing for the
refinancing of outstanding indebtedness of, and additional secured
borrowing by, certain not-for-profit hospitals


 PURPOSE :

To permit certain financially distressed hospitals which have existing
capital, indebtedness under the former "Secured Hospital Loan Program"
to refinance such existing debt and to issue new debt under the
program.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Sections 1 through 10 amend various provisions of the Public Health
Law and Chapter 392 of the Laws of 1973, constituting the NYS Medical
Care Facilities Finance Agency Act, to authorize the refinancing of
existing debt which was issued under the former "secured hospital loan
program" for financially distressed hospitals, and for the issuance of
new tax exempt and/or taxable debt under that program to The Jamaica
Hospital and The Brookdale Hospital Medical Center. These sections
provide that new or refinanced debt for such hospitals will be secured
in the same manner as original debt financed under the program and
also provides that hospitals shall not claim additional Medicaid
reimbursement due to interest payments on refinanced debt.

Section 11 provides that Medicaid reimbursement for interest on debt
refinancing shall be subject to availability of federal financial
participation and that the refinancing of a mortgage loan shall not
alter, affect or change the component of Medicaid rates applicable to
the depreciation of any asset or assets.

Section  12 provides for an immediate effective date.

 EXISTING LAW :

The refinancing of existing indebtedness by, and the issuance of new
debt to, secured hospitals is currently not permitted as the statutory
authorization has expired.

 JUSTIFICATION :

The bill is intended to permit "secured hospitals," and particularly,
two not-for-profit hospitals, previously designated as "financially
distressed," to refinance existing debt and issue new debt upon a
demonstration that the refinancing is undertaken for sound business
purposes and will help improve or maintain the hospital's financial
condition. The "secured hospital loan program" was established to
provide additional support for hospitals identified by the
Commissioner of Health and the Public Health Council as (i) facing
financial distress attributable to significant levels of uncompensated
care, and (ii) nonetheless necessary for the health and safety of
vulnerable populations who otherwise would not have adequate access to
essential services. That program successfully allowed these safety net
facilities to make the capital investments necessary to continue to
serve these populations. While the program expired in 1998,
participating facilities have continued to carry the related debt.

There have been substantial changes in the health care industry since
the program expired, including rapidly increasing health care costs
and dramatically declining hospital margins. In order to continue to
maintain the State's safety net facilities through these troubled
times, the Legislature and Executive have, on occasion, revived the
secured hospital loan program to allow secured facilities to
restructure their debt. This occurred most recently in 2006.

This bill represents another reopening of the program to benefit two
hospitals that participated in the original program. These facilities
have faced unusual challenges in recent years, related not only to the
financial difficulties traditionally facing safety net facilities, but
also to significant closures in their service areas that have
drastically increased the proportion of uncompensated care they must
offer, and that necessitate additional capital investment.
Accordingly, the bill not only allows the refinancing of their
existing debt under the program, but also the issuance of new debt.
Loans made pursuant to this bill may be used for payment of total
hospital project costs, payments of amounts outstanding on existing
mortgage loans, repayment of restructuring loans, payment of operating
costs associated with expansion of capacity to address hospital
closures, refinancing of capital expenses initially funded from
operations, payment of arrears to employee benefit funds, payment
toward professional liability premiums or unfunded professional
liabilities, payment of accumulated historic bad debt and charity care
losses, purchase of an eligible secured hospital borrower's
outstanding special hospital project bonds, or purchase of ancillary
facilities financed by other debt of the eligible secured hospital
borrower or a related entity.

In short, the bill is intended to accomplish two objectives. First,
through prudent refinancing of debt, it will allow the designated
eligible secured hospital borrowers to increase cash flow, pay down
aged payables and otherwise improve their operating position. Second,
the bill has been carefully structured to accomplish these benefits
without unduly burdening the state's Medicaid budget. To this end,
refinancing borrowers must enter into a "Medicaid hold harmless"
agreement with the Commissioner stating that they will not claim
additional interest or depreciation reimbursement beyond amounts that
would have been paid under the preexisting mortgage loan. Thus, the
bill utilizes a proven mechanism to improve the financial condition of
the designated hospitals without inappropriately burdening the State.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

New bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

To be determined.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediate.

A.actClause: AN ACT to amend the public health law and the New York state medical care facilities finance agency act, in relation to providing for the refinancing of outstanding indebtedness of, and additional secured borrowing by, certain not-for-profit hospitals
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S5562A

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the public health law and the New York state medical
care facilities finance agency act, in relation to providing for the
refinancing of outstanding indebtedness of, and additional secured
borrowing by, certain not-for-profit hospitals


 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL :
The purpose of the Bill is to require an orderly process - which
includes adequate notice and advance approval by the Department of
Health -- when an HMO desires to substantially reduce its inpatient
referrals to a hospital on a scale large enough to endanger quality of
care to HMO members and the hospital's ability to serve its local
community.

 SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS :
Section 1. Section 2872 of the public health law is amended by adding
a new subdivision 3-b to read as follows:

3-b. "Eligible secured hospital borrower". A not-for-profit hospital
corporation organized under the laws of this state, which has financed
or refinanced a project or projects pursuant to the former section
seven-a of section one of chapter three hundred ninety-two of the laws
of nineteen hundred seventy-three constituting the New York state
medical care facilities finance agency act, and for which special
hospital project bonds, as defined in former paragraph (d) of
subdivision three of section three of section one of chapter three
hundred ninety-two of the laws of nineteen hundred seventy-three,
remain outstanding and shall also include, for the purposes of making
supplemental mortgage loans as defined in subdivision twelve-a of
section three of section one of chapter three hundred ninety-two of
the laws of nineteen hundred seventy-three, Brookdale Hospital Medical
Center and Jamaica Hospital.

The public health law is amended by adding a new section 2874-b to
read as follows: 2874-b. Refinancing mortgage loans and making
supplemental mortgage loans to eligible secured hospital borrowers.
Eligible secured hospital borrowers, as defined in subdivision three-b
of section twenty-eight hundred seventy-two of this article, shall be
authorized to refinance any mortgage loan financed with the proceeds
of special hospital project bonds, which loans are outstanding as of
the effective date of this section and to finance supplemental
mortgage loans, as defined in subdivision twelve-a of section three of
section one of chapter three hundred ninety-two of the laws of
nineteen hundred seventy-three. A mortgage loan to an eligible secured
hospital borrower, as defined in subdivision three-b of section
twenty-eight hundred seventy-two of this article, or supplemental
mortgage loan, as defined in subdivision twelve-a of section three of
section one of chapter three hundred ninety-two of the laws of
nineteen hundred seventy-three, made by the medical care facilities
finance agency, and any successor thereto, may be financed or
refinanced for a term not longer than the term approved by the
commissioner pursuant to this section or if the bonds issued to
finance such mortgage loan or supplemental mortgage loan are issued as
tax-exempt bonds, such shorter term as is necessary to assure that the
interest on bonds issued to finance or refinance the mortgage loan
will be excludable from the gross income of the holders thereof for
federal tax purposes, provided that in no event shall the term of such
refinancing loan exceed thirty years from the date of the issuance of
the refunding bonds and shall include all costs associated with the
financing or refinancing of indebtedness. All financing or refinancing
applications by eligible secured hospital borrowers shall be approved
by the eligible secured hospital borrower's board and the
commissioner. Such financing or refinancing applications shall include
analytical evidence sufficient to demonstrate that the proposed
financing or refinancing is being undertaken for sound business
purposes and in furtherance of maintaining or improving the financial
condition of the hospital.

 JUSTIFICATION :
The number of patients covered by HMOs is increasing dramatically.
This increase will continue, spurred on by the transformation of the
state Medicaid system to managed care and cost containment pressures
from employers and government at all levels.

As HMO enrollment increases so does an HMO's power to dictate which
hospitals expand and which hospitals shrink or die. In an HMO,
management -- rather than individual physicians or patients -- can
decide where patients are hospitalized. HMOs thus possess a degree of
control over the fate of hospitals that is different from that of any
other non-public entities in New York State.

The potential to exercise this life or death power over hospitals
threatens to disrupt fundamentally the delicate regulatory balance
between access and cost control that is now maintained by the
Department of Health. Hospitals in New York State are operating
generally close to optimum capacity levels. While overall capacity of
hospital services is generally adequate, distribution of that capacity
remains less than ideal. For example, certain inner city and rural
communities still experience access problems. The Department of Health
seeks constantly to maintain and improve the balance between cost
control and access through its statutory authority to set hospital
rates and to determine hospital capacity.

Hospitals are also generally operating close to the edge of financial
solvency. In many communities -- and especially in inner city
neighborhoods -- large institutions that are vital to the communities'
health, cannot survive a substantial drop in the number of admissions
of insured patients. Even in the case of a financially strong
hospital, significant costs and disruption can be avoided if
downsizing occurs in a planned, rational fashion.

Some HMOs are now taking the position that they have no responsibility
to provide notice or plans to a hospital that they have targeted for
termination of a substantial existing referral relationship and that
the Department of Health has no regulatory oversight however severe
the consequences.

A recent example is instructive. Brookdale Hospital Medical Center
("Brookdale") is the largest voluntary hospital in Brooklyn. It has
800 beds, 13 programs for post graduate medical education, more than
200 full time and 400 voluntary attending physicians and over 4000
full time employees (making it the second largest non-governmental
employer in Brooklyn). It has been given "fiscally distressed" status
by the State by virtue of its services to a poor, inner city community
in central and eastern Brooklyn.

For nearly 20 years Brookdale has served as the major hospital for HIP
patients in Brooklyn. In 1992, HIP accounted for over 30% of
Brookdale's admissions. Since early 1993, HIP has been engaged in a
concerted campaign to terminate all referrals to Brookdale despite the
fact that 65% of Brookdale's HIP admissions live in the Hospital's
primary or secondary service areas.  Brookdale has made continual,
good-faith efforts to accommodate HIP's concerns and to negotiate
acceptable compromises; however, at every juncture HIP has proceeded
unilaterally and pursued its plans of abandoning Brookdale.

A total, abrupt pullout of HIP from Brookdale will be devastating to
the hospital's finances and operations. $45 million in 1992 revenues
will be lost to the hospital. Irreparable harm will be 200 beds and to
terminate between 500 and 700 employees. Its teaching programs where
residents in the midst of their clinical education will no longer have
access to the numbers of patients needed to complete their training
may have to be moved to hospitals in other communities. Patterns of
care and existing relationships between Brookdale doctors and their
HIP patients will be broken abruptly.  Most importantly, a vitally
needed community health resource in central Brooklyn maybe lost.

Even if the financial impact of a withdrawal by HIP from Brookdale
could be addressed through State reimbursement relief, there is no
question that many of Brookdale's current programs and services would
need to be significantly cutback or discontinued altogether. There is
also no question that many physicians who currently practice at
Brookdale would be forced to leave the area, resulting in further
aggravating the physician shortage in an already medically underserved
area. Consequently, there are sound policy reasons for requiring that
HIP's withdrawal plans be subject to a public review and approval
process.

In sum, there are three important benefits of this Bill. First, it
will permit rational planning by the appropriate authorities of major
relocations of hospital resources consistent with the existing health
planning policies of New York State. Second, it will prevent major
disruptions of service to all patients, including Medicaid and
uninsured patients, served by a targeted hospital. Third, it will
provide a mechanism to prevent avoidable financial crises.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
1997-98 A.2152

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
There are no direct, significant costs to the State from this
proposal. Indeed, the Bill, if adopted will save state funds. Because
state funds are often the last resort available to protect and assure
the survival of vitally needed hospitals, state funds may ultimately
be needed to compensate for the avoidable damage caused by unplanned,
abrupt terminations of significant hospital HMO relationship.
